extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether a patent's specification satisfies the 35 U.S.C. § 112 written-description requirement (i.e., whether the disclosure demonstrates that the inventor possessed the claimed invention as of the priority/filing date), including related doctrines such as blaze marks, possession, and appellate standard of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (35 U.S.C. § 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The [patent] specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory mandate; purpose is to put the public in possession of what the party claims as his own invention. The AIA amendments do not alter the written-description analysis here. The written-description requirement is a prerequisite for patenting and the 'hallmark' of the requirement is demonstration of possession in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession standard (must convey inventor was in possession)
rubrics_metrics.description: The § 112 written-description requirement is satisfied only if the inventor 'convey[s] with reasonable clarity to those skilled in the art that, as of the filing date sought, he or she was in possession of the invention,' and demonstrate[s] that by disclosure in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession is assessed by an objective inquiry into the four corners of the specification from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSA). A precise definition of the invention is pivotal. Applicant may show possession by describing the invention with all of its limitations using descriptive means (words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating possession by disclosure of all limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may show possession of the claimed invention by describing it with all of its limitations using 'such descriptive means as words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas, etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must disclose the claimed subject matter with sufficient particularity and clarity so that a POSA would understand that the inventor invented what is claimed. Mere aspirational, exploratory, or theoretical research without disclosure of the claimed limitations is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-of-the-art / priority-date focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description is judged based on the state of the art as of the priority date; evidence illuminating the state of the art subsequent to the priority date is not relevant to written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims added later or clinical results obtained after the filing/priority date cannot be used to supply written-description support for an earlier filing date. The inquiry asks what the POSA could deduce from the specification as of the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof; appellate review
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim meets the written-description requirement is a question of fact reviewed for clear error on appeal. Patent invalidity under the written-description doctrine must be established by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District-court fact findings (including witness credibility) receive deference on appeal; appellate courts should not reweigh credibility absent a definite and firm conviction that a mistake was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: When claiming results: express-result claims require adequate support
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor need not prove that a claimed pharmaceutical compound actually achieves a certain result, but when the inventor expressly claims that result, the result must be supported by adequate disclosure in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim expressly recites a therapeutic result (e.g., a therapeutically effective amount for treating a disease), the specification must contain disclosure that supports that asserted result as of the filing date; mere later demonstration of efficacy does not retroactively supply written-description support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blaze-marks doctrine for genus-to-species claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specification discloses a broad genus and the claims recite a particular species within that genus, the specification must provide sufficient 'blaze marks' to guide a reader through the disclosed possibilities toward the claimed species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laundry-list or broad genus disclosures without guidance are insufficient to support species claims. Blaze marks are required when the disclosure is a large number of unmarked possibilities; if the specification specifically points out the claimed species (or otherwise provides guidance), blaze marks may be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating written description with obviousness/POSA expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The written-description inquiry is distinct from obviousness; what a POSA would expect regarding success from the prior art (obviousness context) should not be overlaid onto the written-description inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description asks whether the specification demonstrates possession as of the filing date, not whether a POSA would have expected the claimed invention to be successful based on prior-art analysis. Caution: statements about POSA expectations may be relevant only insofar as they reflect what the specification itself would have taught a POSA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific claim limitations (e.g., dosages, indications) require linking disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a specific parameter (such as a particular dosage for a therapeutic indication) must be supported by the specification such that a POSA would understand that the inventor possessed that specific parameter for the claimed use as of the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single, passing mention of a specific dose buried in a broad range and not linked to the claimed indication may be insufficient. Anti-patterns: (1) listing broad ranges labeled 'effective' without tying particular values to the claimed therapeutic effect; (2) 'anchoring' a particular dose among broad ranges that also include known-ineffective or implausible doses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective inquiry into the specification as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter; the inquiry considers the specification as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolated passages must be read in context. The court will assess the overall disclosure (methods, examples, definitions, figures) to determine whether the claimed invention is supported. However, selecting only selectively plucked disclosures to assemble claim support is disfavored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and factual findings matter in bench trials
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts' credibility determinations and factual findings (e.g., expert testimony regarding how a POSA would read the specification) are entitled to substantial deference on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate courts should not disturb the district court's credibility assessments absent clear error; the district court's firsthand assessment of live witness testimony can be decisive in close written-description disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification definitions affect scope of claimed terms
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification defines a claim term (e.g., 'therapeutically effective amount'), that definition informs the written-description inquiry and what a POSA would understand the claim to mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions in the specification that tie claimed terms to certain outcomes (clinical or biological) will shape whether the disclosure supports the claimed result; parties cannot later recharacterize the meaning inconsistent with the specification to cure a written-description defect.
